disclaimer: Demonstration dataset. Route paths, waypoint years, group structure and pacing are ILLUSTRATIVE visual reconstructions. Site dates and the cited literature are the evidence layer; site coordinates are approximate. Citations should be reviewed by a domain specialist and the routes replaced with research-backed data before publication.

routes.name: Africa → Levant
routes.uncertainty: Homo sapiens was in the Levant by ~120,000–90,000 years ago, but the path out of Africa and the timing drawn here are illustrative. Whether these groups left lasting descendants is debated.
routes.pathDescription: Drawn northward along the Nile corridor and across Sinai. A southern crossing at Bab-el-Mandeb is also discussed in the literature.
routes.description: Fossils show Homo sapiens in the southern Levant long before the main out-of-Africa dispersal.
routes.people: Early Homo sapiens hunter-gatherers from northeast Africa. Nothing is known about their language or social identity.
routes.historicalContext: The Last Interglacial (~130,000–115,000 years ago) brought wetter phases that periodically made the Sahara and Sinai more passable.
routes.significance: Shows that leaving Africa was not a single event; our species ranged into Southwest Asia repeatedly, sometimes sharing the region with Neanderthals.

evidence.description: Homo sapiens burials at Skhul and Qafzeh (Israel), dated roughly 90,000–130,000 years ago.
The Misliya Cave maxilla (~177,000–194,000 years ago) hints at even earlier, possibly intermittent, presence.
Most non-African ancestry traces to a later dispersal, so the genetic legacy of these early groups is unclear.

routes.name: Africa → South Asia
routes.uncertainty: Genetics strongly supports a major dispersal ~70,000–50,000 years ago, but its exact timing and whether it left via Bab-el-Mandeb or Sinai are debated. This coastal path is illustrative.
routes.pathDescription: Drawn across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait and along the Arabian and Iranian coasts, following the 'southern route' hypothesis.
routes.description: The dispersal from which most present-day non-African populations descend.
routes.people: Homo sapiens hunter-gatherers from northeast Africa, probably in small, mobile groups. Their specific identity is unknown.
routes.historicalContext: A glacial world with sea levels well below today's, narrowing the Bab-el-Mandeb strait and exposing coastal shelves now under water.
routes.significance: Ancestors of most people outside Africa took part in this dispersal, and shortly after it they interbred with Neanderthals.

evidence.description: Genome-wide data show most non-African populations derive from a dispersal roughly 50,000–70,000 years ago.
The 45,000-year-old Ust'-Ishim genome dates Neanderthal admixture to roughly 50,000–60,000 years ago.
Stone tools at Jwalapuram (India) bracket the ~74,000-year-old Toba eruption; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated.
Models link the timing of dispersal to climatic and technological change in Africa.

routes.name: Southwest Asia → Europe
routes.uncertainty: Homo sapiens is well attested in Europe by ~45,000 years ago. The Danube corridor drawn here is one plausible path; earlier incursions such as Grotte Mandrin (~54,000 years ago) are debated and not shown as a separate wave.
routes.pathDescription: Drawn across Anatolia and Thrace, then westward along the Danube corridor into central and western Europe.
routes.description: Homo sapiens spreads into a continent already occupied by Neanderthals.
routes.people: Homo sapiens hunter-gatherers carrying early Upper Palaeolithic technologies. Several early groups left little ancestry in later Europeans.
routes.historicalContext: A cold, climatically unstable phase of the last glacial period; Neanderthals disappear from the record over the following millennia.
routes.significance: Marks the overlap and eventual replacement of Neanderthals in Europe, and the start of Europe's Upper Palaeolithic.

evidence.description: Homo sapiens remains at Bacho Kiro Cave (Bulgaria), ~46,000–44,000 years ago.
A modern-human tooth and tools at Grotte Mandrin (France) are dated ~54,000 years ago; the interpretation is debated.
Ancient genomes show a complex history of early European populations, several with little lasting legacy.

routes.name: Southwest Asia → Caucasus
routes.uncertainty: Upper Palaeolithic occupation of the southern Caucasus is dated to roughly 42,000–38,000 years ago; where these groups came from and the path drawn here are illustrative.
routes.pathDescription: Drawn north through the uplands of eastern Anatolia and the Armenian Highlands into the valleys of the southern Caucasus.
routes.description: Homo sapiens reaches the mountain valleys of the southern Caucasus, another former Neanderthal region.
routes.people: Upper Palaeolithic Homo sapiens hunter-gatherers. No specific identity can be assigned.
routes.historicalContext: Neanderthal occupation of the region ends around the same time Upper Palaeolithic sites appear.
routes.significance: The Caucasus links Southwest Asia with the steppe; later genomes from here help explain West Eurasian ancestry.

evidence.description: Ortvale Klde rockshelter (Georgia) records the shift to Upper Palaeolithic occupation ~42,000–38,000 years ago.
~26,000-year-old genomes from Dzudzuana Cave suggest deep links between Caucasus and Near Eastern populations (preprint).

routes.name: Southeast Asia → Sahul

branches.name: Northern route (via Sulawesi)
branches.note: Northern (Sulawesi–Maluku) and southern (Timor) crossings into Sahul are both proposed; neither is established.

routes.uncertainty: Arrival in Sahul is dated anywhere from ~65,000 to ~50,000 years ago depending on the site and method; this is actively debated. The island-hopping path is one of several proposed.
routes.pathDescription: Drawn down the exposed Sunda Shelf and through the Lesser Sunda Islands, where open-sea crossings were unavoidable, to the Sahul Shelf.
routes.description: The first people to reach Australia and New Guinea, which required repeated sea crossings.
routes.people: Homo sapiens hunter-gatherers moving through island Southeast Asia, ancestral to Aboriginal Australians and Papuans.
routes.historicalContext: Low glacial sea levels joined western Indonesia into the continent of Sunda and Australia–New Guinea into Sahul; the Wallacean islands between them were never connected by land.
routes.significance: Among the earliest evidence of deliberate open-water voyaging by humans.

evidence.description: Madjedbebe (northern Australia) has been dated to ~65,000 years ago; others argue for ~50,000 or less.
A modern human skull from Tam Pa Ling (Laos) is dated to at least ~46,000 years ago.
Burials at Lake Mungo show people deep in the Australian interior by ~42,000 years ago.
Aboriginal Australian genomes indicate a long, separate history after a shared out-of-Africa origin.
Reconstructed coastlines show Wallacea required multiple sea crossings even at low sea level.

routes.name: Asia → Beringia → Americas

branches.name: Interior route (debated)
branches.note: An inland route east of the Rocky Mountains depended on when an ice-free corridor opened; its timing relative to the first arrivals is debated.

routes.uncertainty: People were in South America by ~14,500 years ago. Earlier arrivals (e.g. White Sands footprints, ~23,000–21,000 years ago) and the coastal vs. ice-free-corridor route are debated. Pacing here is illustrative.
routes.pathDescription: Drawn across the exposed Bering land bridge, slowing in Beringia (the 'standstill'), then down the Pacific coast to South America.
routes.description: The last continental landmasses settled by Homo sapiens before the Holocene.
routes.people: Homo sapiens from northeast Asia; the ancestors of Indigenous peoples of the Americas.
routes.historicalContext: The Last Glacial Maximum: ice sheets covered much of North America, and low sea level exposed a broad land bridge between Asia and Alaska.
routes.significance: Completes the dispersal of Homo sapiens across every continent except Antarctica.

evidence.description: Yana RHS shows people in Arctic Siberia ~32,000 years ago.
Monte Verde (Chile) is occupied by ~14,500 years ago.
Footprints at White Sands (New Mexico) dated ~23,000–21,000 years ago; the dating is debated.
Mitochondrial lineages suggest a period of isolation in Beringia before rapid spread south.
An ancient Alaskan genome reveals a founding 'Ancient Beringian' population.
Ice sheets peaked ~26,000–19,000 years ago, shaping when routes south were open.
